title: The Infants' Praise and Christ's Mount
english: …meditation, patience, and endurance. “He has blessed your children within you” (Psalm 147:13). These are the faithful infants who received the Lord with the branches, that is, with new fruits, who nurse on the milk of Christ’s teaching. For as soon as they believe in Him, they praise, they sing hymns, they give glory, as it is written: “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies You have prepared praise” (Psalm 8:2; Matthew 21:16).

Let us become a holy mount for Him in place of the unclean colt, so that He may ride upon us. Let us yoke the chariot of our thoughts to Him, “and He will reign” over us “forever, and of His kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:33).

Let us take up a cheerful way of life like olive branches, “to make our face cheerful with oil” (Psalm 104:15), as the psalmist says, and again: “Serve the Lord with gladness” (Psalm 100:2). Again, let us carry in the inner man the divine and spiritual…
translator_notes: The section opens in the middle of the list that ends the previous section (the bars of the gates: faith, hope, love…), and ends in the middle of a sentence completed at the start of the next section (“…work”).

Psalm 147:13 is Psalm 147:2 in the Septuagint; “children” renders “sons”, as standard English versions do, because the next clause explains them as infants. Psalm 8:2 is 8:3 in the Septuagint, as quoted in Matthew 21:16; Psalm 104:15 is 103:15; Psalm 100:2 is 99:2.
Luke 1:33 is Gabriel’s promise, adapted from “over the house of Jacob” to “over us”; only the quoted words sit inside the quotation marks.
“Mount” renders a word for a thing one rides, set against the unclean colt. “Chariot” picks up “the chariots of Ephraim” earlier in the homily.
Hesychius plays on “cheerful” (a cheerful way of life; to make the face cheerful) and on olive and oil; the English keeps both links. “Inner man” is the term used earlier in the homily.

title: Palm Branches of Faith, Hope, and Love
english: …work, like the branches of the palm trees (John 12:13), and let us follow Him, giving thanks to Him. Instead of their whiteness, let us carry right, undefiled, and simple faith; instead of their sharpness, patient hope, which pierces and slays every thought that rises up to take us captive away from the knowledge of God (2 Corinthians 10:5); and instead of the sweetness of the palm, sweet love, which is made up of the faith and hope already named and the rest, so that what was said may be fulfilled in us: “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree; he will grow like a cedar in Lebanon” (Psalm 92:12).

Let us follow Him into the holy city; let us enter the temple with Him, so that He may overturn the tables of the money changers within us and drive away from us the demons who sell the doves (Matthew 21:12), the thoughts that fly about in error, together with…
translator_notes: The section opens with the noun (“work”) that completes the last sentence of the previous section, and ends in the middle of a sentence that the next section completes.
Hesychius draws faith, hope, and love from the whiteness, the sharp points, and the sweet fruit of the palm.
Psalm 92:12 is Psalm 91:13 in the Septuagint.

title: A Holy Temple for Christ
english: …all who sell and buy among us, and that, instead of a den of robbers (Matthew 21:13), He may make us a holy temple, like the temple of old, in which Christ dwells and walks (2 Corinthians 6:16); so that He may grant light to the blind in us, make the deaf hear and the lame walk (Matthew 11:5), and raise the dead with Lazarus—for where life dwells, there is resurrection—so that with Lazarus and the crowds and His disciples, with infants and nursing babies, and with the holy angels, we may cry aloud, shouting: “Hosanna in the highest; blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 118:26; Matthew 21:9), Christ, Lord and God, “the King of the ages” (1 Timothy 1:17). To Him be glory, honor, and worship, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
translator_notes: The section completes the sentence begun in the previous section and ends the homily.
Psalm 118:26 is Psalm 117:26 in the Septuagint.
